newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt opposes Israel's Hebron demands.
newsitem.headline: Egypt opposes Israel's Hebron demands.

text.p: Egypt said on Tuesday that Israel's demands in talks with the Palestinians on Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron were unacceptable, illogical and likely to lead to revenge and violence.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak told reporters in the Suez Canal town of Qantara that the Israeli idea of setting aside streets in Hebron for Jewish settlers, for example, was worse than the apartheid system in the old South Africa.

"(One) point is the Shuhada road (a Hebron street), which looks like much more than apartheid. You cannot say that this road is only for the settlers and the Jews and the Palestinians are not allowed to pass through.
"It is impossible, unacceptable and logically very dangerous," he said.
He also objected to the Israeli demand for the right of "hot pursuit" into parts of Hebron under nominal Palestinian control.

"This hot pursuit in the future...is going to create a hell of a problem, a hell of a lot of violence, because the Palestinian will never accept the Israeli authority coming there and inspecting his house and taking him to Israel.
"Then violence and revenge will start again, that means we are going to reach nowhere. It will never be accepted," he said.
But Mubarak also said there was no going back on progress towards peace in the Middle East, whatever the rightwing government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wanted.

"There's no escape from the peace process. There are obstacles from time to time but there's no retreat from peace, because a retreat from peace is a very big disaster, even for the forces which are against peace," he said.

"We have to keep going... The peace process won't stop, whether we want it or not, whether Israel wants it or not. The Israeli side is putting obstacles...which make it difficult for the Palestinians to accept these conditions," he added.

Talks on Hebron, home to 400 Jewish settlers and 100,000 Palestinians, have reached stalemate over Netanyahu's insistence his troops be allowed to enter parts of the city under Palestinian control in "hot pursuit" of suspected guerrillas.

Israel and the Palestinians reached an agreement with the former Israeli government on the Hebron redeployment more than a year ago but Netanyahu, who was elected in May, has been trying to renegotiate the deal.
Mubarak has said he will not meet Netanyahu again until he satisfies Palestinian demands in the Hebron talks.

"There should be a formula and the Israelis should respond to the needs and respect what was signed before," he said in Qantara, where he was inaugurating a project to pipe Nile water under the Suez Canal to irrigate north Sinai.
